newsitem.title: USA: Clinton speech, O.J. verdict a hard call for TV.
newsitem.headline: Clinton speech, O.J. verdict a hard call for TV.

text.p: U.S. television networks scrambled on Tuesday to deal simultaneously with matters of state and affairs of the flesh as President Bill Clinton's State of the Union address coincided with the drama of the O.J. Simpson verdict.
For a while, it looked like live broadcasting's Armageddon as two major events competed for the nation's attention.
In Santa Monica, California, the jury was about to declare the former football star liable for the deaths of his ex-wife and her friend after a four-month civil trial and six days of deliberations.
In Washington, Clinton was ready to deliver to Congress an hour-long speech on the state of the nation, the theme and contents of which already had been widely discussed and analysed.
Would the networks opt for excitement and suspense or the famously loquacious president doing his Constitutional duty?

"We're going to keep you absolutely up to date with what's going to happen," ABC's Peter Jennings assured television viewers as split screen images showed the boisterous scene outside the California court and the solemn gathering in the House of Representatives chamber.

NBC decided at 8.59 p.m. -- one minute before Clinton's speech was scheduled to begin -- that it would stick with the address, but said the network's cable station MSNBC would switch to O.J. Simpson coverage instead.

Anchorman Dan Rather, indicating just how much the networks were sweating over the unexpected challenge, took pains to explain that CBS would honour its commitment to broadcast Clinton, but would run "crawls" on the verdict -- printed text on the screen.
In the end, the verdict was read in Santa Monica just moments before Clinton wound up his speech on Capitol Hill.
Most of the networks opted for "crawls," which meant the president's image was squashed into two-thirds of the screen to make room for a stream of words about the verdict.

CBS, however, moved the State of the Union coverage to a tiny box in the corner and printed the jury's decision in oversize type. It also scrapped plans to immediately televise the Republican response and chose instead to give a news briefing on the Simpson trial decision.
ABC managed to marry the two stories earlier with a live interview of Representative Jesse Jackson Jr. in which the Chicago Democrat was asked about the impact of the impending Simpson verdict.
"It's clear as the president focuses on building a bridge to the 21st century, the O.J. Simpson verdict has made the issue of race a central factor in building that bridge," Jackson said.

The White House became somewhat testy when asked if Clinton had considered delaying his speech until the verdict was read. After all, the date already had been changed once to avoid conflict with the TV broadcast of the Miss USA beauty pageant on Wednesday night.
"Absolutely not," spokesman Mike McCurry replied sharply. "We're fulfilling our Constitutional obligation."

The White House clearly feared the TV networks would preempt Clinton's speech in favour of the more exciting Simpson verdict. But McCurry again declared "absolutely not" when asked if the court had been requested to delay announcement of the jury's decision.
